newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Iran submarines still have problems-French admiral.
newsitem.headline: Iran submarines still have problems-French admiral.

text.p: Iran's submarine force is still facing operational difficulties but it now has the capability to permanently patrol the Gulf's vital oil export routes, a French naval commander said on Sunday.

Iran "does not have a very strong submarine today, they have problems...It is very difficult to form a submarine force from nothing," said Rear-Admiral Stephane Legris de la Salle, commander of French naval forces in the Indian Ocean region.
"The fact is that there are three Iranian submarines...and this adds a new dimension in case of crisis or war...It changes the vision of the area," he told Reuters in an interview.

Iran has taken delivery of three Kilo-class submarines from Russia since 1992, becoming the only regional state to deploy such vessels in an area which controls almost 70 percent of the world's oil reserves. The third one was delivered in January.

"With only two submarines one is in repair and the other is at sea. If you have a problem (breakdown) this is it, but with three submarines they can permanently have one at sea," added the French commnader.
But he stopped short of echoing concern often voiced by Western military officials that Iran is a potential threat to neighbouring Gulf states and the free flow of oil through the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran shares the Hormuz, the only entrance to the Gulf through which some 15 million barrels of oil are exported daily, with Oman.
Some Western officers say Iran could use the submarines to lay mines but Legris de la Salle said even a fishing vessel could carry out a similar mission in the Hormuz by night.
Iran is opposed to the presence of non-Gulf powers in the area, mainly forces from the United States, France and Britain.
But like other officers serving on warships in the region, the French commander said exchanges with the Iranian navy and Iranian authorities when crossing the Hormuz were cordial and professional.
"It is peacetime and international (maritime) law applies. We respect them (Iranian navy) and we cross freely. No problems at all," he said.
But the Iranian submarines were of concern, he said.

High salinity and a large difference in temperature between the surface and the seabed made it difficult to detect the Iranian submarines which need experience to operate in shallow Gulf waters busy with oil tanker traffic.

"It is very difficult to find a submarine even if it is not a very good one and the submarine crew is not very well-trained," he said. "Sound propagation is very difficult (in the Gulf) and you have to depend on the sound and your ears".
